List of public art in Denver

stops.name: Colorado State Capitol
stops.description: Its dome carries real gold leaf laid in 1908 for the state's mining history, and a marker on the west steps puts you at exactly one mile above sea level - though surveys moved the true spot from the 15th step to the 13th.

stops.name: Civic Center Park
stops.description: A National Historic Landmark since 2012 and one of the country's best surviving pieces of City Beautiful planning, with a Greek amphitheater at one end and the Voorhies Memorial seal pond at the other.

stops.name: Denver City and County Building
stops.description: Deliberately built low in 1932 so it would not block the Capitol's view of the mountains, this Greek Revival crescent closes the west end of Civic Center Park facing the gold dome.

stops.name: Denver Art Museum
stops.description: Two architects' only American buildings stand side by side here: Gio Ponti's 24-sided tower clad in a million reflective tiles, and Daniel Libeskind's titanium wedge of 2006.

stops.name: Byers-Evans House
stops.description: Built in 1883 by the founder of the Rocky Mountain News, lived in by the Evans family until 1981, and still holding roughly 90 percent of its original furnishings.

stops.name: Denver Mint
stops.description: Modeled on a Florentine palazzo and striking coins since 1906, this is the largest coin producer in the world - every US coin stamped with a D was made behind these walls.

stops.name: Denver Municipal Auditorium
stops.description: Opened in 1908 as the second-largest venue in America after Madison Square Garden, it hosted that year's Democratic National Convention and Led Zeppelin's first US concert in 1968; it is the Ellie Caulkins Opera House today.

stops.name: Denver Athletic Club
stops.description: A Romanesque Revival block from 1889 housing a private club founded in 1884, helped into existence by John Elitch of Elitch Gardens fame.

stops.name: Denver Press Club
stops.description: The oldest press club in the country, incorporated in 1877, whose basement poker room still carries a 1945 Herndon Davis mural of the Denver newsmen who drank there.

stops.name: Daniels and Fisher Tower
stops.description: Copied from the campanile in Venice's Piazza San Marco and finished in 1910, it was the tallest building between the Mississippi and California, and outlived by a decade the department store it was built to advertise.

stops.name: Colorado National Bank Building
stops.description: The 1915 marble banking hall is a hotel lobby now, and the 16 Allen Tupper True murals painted here in the 1920s were kept in place through the conversion, along with three of the original vaults.

stops.name: Equitable Building
stops.description: Denver's tallest building from 1892 until the Daniels and Fisher Tower passed it, nine floors of arched windows and carved granite once served by eight elevators run off an artesian well in the basement.

stops.name: Brown Palace Hotel
stops.description: A wedge of sandstone and red granite squeezed into a flatiron corner in 1892, and one of the first hotels anywhere built around an open atrium under stained glass.

stops.name: Trinity United Methodist Church
stops.description: Its 181-foot Gothic spire made it the tallest thing in Denver when it opened in 1887, and the sanctuary still holds a 4,290-pipe Roosevelt organ.

note: READ THIS FIRST - the run history in git is not what it looks like. This morning origin/main was force-updated and now points at a line of history that contains only four nightly runs (Atlanta twice, Dallas, Cleveland). The line it replaced, still present locally at commit b85111f, holds six more runs that are no longer reachable from main: Baltimore 2026-07-30, Boston 07-31, Buffalo 08-01, Charlotte 08-02, Chicago 08-03, Cincinnati 08-04. I picked Baltimore first off main's visible history, caught the discrepancy, and switched to Denver, which has never run on either line. Anything deriving a city rotation or a last-run timestamp from main's log alone will now believe those six cities are untouched - worth a human deciding whether that history should be restored. Denver stops form a downtown loop of roughly two miles: Civic Center at the south end (Capitol, City and County Building, Art Museum, Byers-Evans, Mint), north up Glenarm past the two clubs, out to the Daniels and Fisher Tower on the 16th Street Mall, then back down the 17th Street bank row to the Brown Palace and Trinity. Every address came from the NRHP row or the venue itself and every ZIP was looked up independently; none is null. Nothing was dropped as demolished, but two stops are survivors worth knowing about - the Daniels and Fisher department store came down around 1971 and only its tower stands, and the Municipal Auditorium's 1953 arena half was demolished in 1990 while the 1908 auditorium became the opera house. The Equitable Building's article does not say what the building is used for today, so its description stays with what is verifiable. Left out only to keep the loop walkable, all strong and all close: Denver Union Station, the Molly Brown House, the Cathedral Basilica of the Immaculate Conception, the Colorado Governor's Mansion and the Boston Building. Union Station plus LoDo is the obvious next Denver batch.
